script.opening: "My right ear’s been sore and itchy for a few days, with some discharge. It hurts if I touch it or pull on it, and feels blocked, muffled. I’ve been poking it with cotton buds to clean it, and I was swimming last week. Can you sort it?"

facts.text: Right ear, 4 days. Itchy first, then sore — "five out of ten", worse lying on it and when he touches or pulls the ear. Yellowish crusty discharge, no blood. Feels blocked and muffled.
Saw the practice nurse this morning for his blood pressure; she looked in the ear: "She said the canal was red, swollen and full of gunk and she couldn’t see the eardrum." His BP was fine.

No fever, feels well. No severe pain at night. No dizziness, no facial weakness, no ringing. No swelling behind the ear or spreading redness on the face. Never had ear surgery or a perforated eardrum. No previous ear infections as an adult.
Uses cotton buds every day after a shower, "to get the wax out". Swims three times a week at the leisure centre. Has mild eczema on his hands, sometimes in his ears.
Not diabetic as far as he knows; no immune problems. Takes ramipril for blood pressure. No allergies.
Call-centre team leader — wears a headset all day. Lives with wife and teenage daughter.

Relaxed, a bit impatient — wants it sorted quickly. Expect antibiotic tablets ("So I don’t need tablets?"). Ask how to put drops in properly, and whether you can keep swimming. Admit cotton buds are "an old habit".

ice.ideas: "An infection. I thought I’d need antibiotics to get rid of it quickly."
ice.concerns: "Whether the hearing will come back properly — I need it for work."

cues: "I’ve been poking it with cotton buds" — the habit that keeps it going.
"I was swimming last week" — water exposure; advice on keeping the ear dry.
"So I don’t need tablets?" — expectation of oral antibiotics to discuss.

checkpoints.text: Recognises OTITIS EXTERNA — ear pain/itch/discharge, PAIN ON MOVING the tragus/pinna, a red/swollen/debris-filled canal, provoked by water/swimming and cotton-bud trauma
Distinguishes it from otitis MEDIA and considers foreign body, furuncle and fungal OE (otomycosis)

Manages uncomplicated OE correctly (UKHSA 2025) — analgesia and heat, aural toilet, topical acetic acid or antibiotic +/- steroid drops/spray (not systemic; aminoglycoside caution if the drum is perforated or unseen), keep DRY, ear wick if very swollen — reserving oral flucloxacillin with referral for spreading cellulitis/systemic involvement
Advises PREVENTION/technique — STOP cotton buds, keep ears dry, treat skin conditions, correct drop technique — and addresses recurrent causes

Screens MALIGNANT (NECROTISING) OE red flags in high-risk patients (elderly diabetic/immunocompromised): severe pain out of proportion/worse at night, granulation, facial palsy — and would refer URGENTLY to ENT
Explains the diagnosis and why topical (not oral) treatment is appropriate, engaging him in keep-dry/stop-cotton-buds advice without dismissiveness
Checks understanding of drop technique and prevention, and responds to his wish for quick relief realistically
Safety-nets and follows up: review if not improving/spreading, malignant-OE red flags warranting urgent ENT (esp. diabetics), prevention to avoid recurrence

worked.txt: (After a face-to-face look in the ear.) "You’ve got otitis externa — inflammation of the ear canal. The swimming and, honestly, the cotton buds set it off: the buds scratch the canal and push stuff in, which keeps it going. It usually settles well with the right drops."

"First, painkillers and a warm compress for the pain. Then ear DROPS — either an acidic drop or an antibiotic with a steroid, which work about as well as each other at a week — rather than antibiotic tablets, which aren’t needed. Use them for about seven days. I’ll check whether your eardrum is intact, as that decides which drops are safe. I’ll clean the ear so the drops get in. If the canal’s too swollen, we sometimes place a little wick."
"Use the drops lying with the bad ear up and stay still a few minutes. Crucially: stop the cotton buds completely, and keep the ear dry — no swimming while it settles, keep water out in the shower."
"Once better, keeping ears dry and leaving them alone prevents most recurrences. If you’re a keen swimmer we can talk about keeping water out."

(If high-risk/severe:) "Because severe ear infections can occasionally become serious — especially with diabetes — severe pain worse at night and out of proportion, or any facial weakness, would need urgent ENT. That doesn’t fit you now, but worth knowing."
"Come back if it’s not improving in a week, the pain gets much worse, it spreads to the skin around the ear, or you feel feverish. Otherwise the drops and keeping it dry should sort it."

f.learning: OTITIS EXTERNA (inflammation of the external ear CANAL) presents with ear PAIN, ITCH and DISCHARGE, PAIN ON MOVING the tragus/pinna, and a blocked/muffled-hearing sensation, with a red, swollen, debris-filled canal; it is provoked by WATER/SWIMMING ("swimmer’s ear"), local TRAUMA (cotton buds), and skin conditions (eczema/seborrhoeic dermatitis/psoriasis). Distinguish it from otitis MEDIA (deeper pain, systemic/febrile especially in children, a bulging/red drum, no tragal tenderness; discharge if the drum perforates), and consider a foreign body, a furuncle, and FUNGAL OE/otomycosis (itch-predominant, fungal debris, may need antifungal drops). Manage uncomplicated OE: adequate ANALGESIA, AURAL TOILET (cleaning/microsuction improves drop delivery), analgesia and local heat first, then topical ACETIC ACID (over 12s) or a TOPICAL antibiotic +/- corticosteroid (similar cure rates at 7 days — UKHSA Summary of antimicrobial prescribing guidance 2025; choice per BNF) rather than systemic antibiotics, avoiding aminoglycoside drops if the drum is perforated or cannot be seen unless the ENT UK criteria are met, keeping the ear DRY (avoid water/swimming during treatment) and using an ear WICK (ENT) if the canal is very swollen; reserve oral flucloxacillin, with referral to exclude necrotising OE, for cellulitis spreading beyond the canal or systemic signs. Advise prevention and technique — STOP cotton buds (they cause trauma and push debris in), keep ears dry, treat underlying skin conditions, and use drops correctly. The critical RED FLAG is MALIGNANT (NECROTISING) OTITIS EXTERNA in a high-risk patient (elderly DIABETIC or immunocompromised): SEVERE, persistent pain (out of proportion, worse at night), copious discharge, GRANULATION tissue in the canal, and/or cranial-nerve involvement (e.g. facial palsy) — a skull-base osteomyelitis that is serious/potentially life-threatening and needs same-day ENT/hospital referral (UK consensus 2023), imaging and IV antibiotics, not routine OE treatment. The skill is correct topical management, advice/technique, and screening the malignant-OE red flags; otoscopy needs a face-to-face appointment.

knowledge.summary: Pain on moving the tragus, itch, discharge and a swollen, debris-filled canal after swimming and cotton-bud use is acute otitis externa. Treat topically, clean the canal so the drops reach it, keep it dry and stop the cotton buds. Oral antibiotics are for spreading cellulitis or systemic illness, and severe persistent pain in a diabetic or immunocompromised person raises necrotising otitis externa.

points.t: Otalgia, itch, discharge, a blocked or muffled feeling, and pain on moving the tragus or pinna, with a red, swollen canal containing debris. Triggers: swimming and water exposure, trauma from cotton buds or fingers, hearing aids or earplugs, and skin conditions such as eczema, seborrhoeic dermatitis or psoriasis.

Otitis media gives deeper pain, often with a bulging or red drum and no tragal tenderness; discharge only follows a perforation. Also consider a furuncle (focal boil), a foreign body, and otomycosis (itch, fluffy white or black debris), which needs antifungal drops rather than antibiotics.

UKHSA summary [1]: analgesia and local heat; then topical acetic acid (over 12s) or a topical antibiotic with or without a steroid, which have similar cure rates at 7 days. Cochrane [4]: acetic acid is comparable at 1 week but less effective when treatment is longer. Choice and dosing per BNF. Do not give oral antibiotics for uncomplicated otitis externa [1][5].

Remove debris by dry mopping or refer for microsuction if the canal is blocked; a very swollen canal may need an ear wick placed by ENT or a trained clinician. Lie with the affected ear up for a few minutes after the drops go in.

If the drum is perforated or cannot be seen, avoid aminoglycoside drops unless ENT specifically advises them; the ENT UK consensus conditions (obvious infection, no more than 2 weeks, risks explained, ideally baseline audiometry) are a specialist exception [2]. Use a non-aminoglycoside preparation instead (per BNF and local formulary).
UKHSA summary [1]: if cellulitis spreads beyond the canal or there are systemic signs, give oral flucloxacillin (dose per BNF) and refer to exclude necrotising otitis externa.

UK consensus [3]: suspect it in people with diabetes, immunosuppression or older age who have severe or persistent pain (often worse at night) out of proportion to the signs, granulation tissue in the canal, or cranial nerve palsy, especially facial. It is a skull-base osteomyelitis needing same-day ENT assessment.

Stop cotton buds; keep the ear dry (no swimming until settled, protect the ear when showering); treat any canal eczema; after recovery, consider earplugs or a swimming cap and drying the ear gently. Recurrent or non-resolving disease needs review and ENT referral.

model.text: Hello Mr Pryce, I’m Dr Evans. Come and have a seat. What’s brought you in?

My right ear’s been sore and itchy for a few days, with some discharge. It hurts if I touch it or pull on it, and it feels blocked, muffled. I’ve been poking it with cotton buds to clean it, and I was swimming last week. Can you sort it?
That sounds really uncomfortable. I’ll do my best to sort it. Let me ask a few things and then have a look inside.
How bad is the pain, and is it worse at any particular time, for example at night?
model.why: Severity and night pain, a necrotising OE marker

model.text: Sore, maybe five out of ten. Worse when I lie on it. Not keeping me up.
What does the discharge look like? Any blood?
Yellowish, a bit crusty. No blood.
Any fever, or feeling unwell in yourself? Any redness or swelling spreading onto the outside of the ear or your face?
No, I feel fine otherwise.
Any weakness of your face, dizziness or ringing in the ear?
model.why: Screens facial palsy and inner ear involvement

model.text: No.
Have you had diabetes, any problem with your immune system, or any treatment that lowers immunity? Any eczema or psoriasis?
model.why: Risk factors for necrotising OE and skin triggers

model.text: Not that I know of.
Have you had ear problems before, a perforated eardrum or ear operations? Do you use hearing aids or earplugs?
No, nothing like that.
What did you think was going on, and what were you hoping I’d do?
An infection. I thought I’d need antibiotics to get rid of it quickly.
That makes sense. Is anything else worrying you about it?
Just whether the hearing will come back.

Let me look. I’ll pull gently on the ear first … that’s sore, isn’t it? The canal is red and swollen and there’s debris in it, so it’s hard to see the eardrum clearly. You don’t have a temperature and the skin around the ear looks normal.
model.why: Tragal tenderness, otoscopy, spreading cellulitis excluded

model.text: So what is it?

It’s otitis externa, an inflammation and infection of the skin of the ear canal. Swimming softens the skin, and the cotton buds scratch it and push debris further in, which keeps it going. The muffled hearing is from the swelling and debris, and it should come back as it settles.
model.why: Diagnosis linked to triggers; answers the hearing concern

model.text: So I don’t need tablets?

Tablets aren’t the best treatment here. Drops or a spray put the treatment right where the infection is, at a much higher strength, and they work better for this. Antibiotic tablets are for when infection spreads to the skin outside the ear or makes you unwell, and that isn’t the case.
model.why: Topical over systemic, with the reason

model.text: Okay, that makes sense.

I’ll gently clean out the debris now so the drops can reach the skin. Because I can’t see your eardrum clearly, I’ll choose drops that are safe even if there were a small hole in it. Use them for a week. Paracetamol or ibuprofen will help the pain, and a warm flannel against the ear can soothe it.
model.why: Aural toilet; safe choice when the drum is not seen; analgesia

model.text: How do I put them in properly?

Lie on your side with the sore ear up, put the drops in, then gently press on the flap in front of the ear a few times and stay still for a few minutes. If the canal swells shut and the drops won’t go in, come back, because we may need to place a small wick or get ENT to clean it.
model.why: Drop technique and wick if needed

model.text: And the swimming?

No swimming until it has fully settled, and keep water out when you shower, for example with cotton wool coated in petroleum jelly. Most importantly, no more cotton buds at all. The ear cleans itself. Could you manage that?
I’ll try. Old habit.

Come back if it isn’t clearly better after a week of drops, if the pain gets much worse or keeps you awake at night, if redness spreads onto your ear or face, if you feel feverish, or if you notice any weakness of your face. Those need checking the same day.
model.why: Specific safety-net including necrotising OE features

model.text: Okay. Drops for a week, lie with the ear up, no cotton buds, keep it dry, come back if it’s worse.
That’s it exactly. If your hearing hasn’t fully returned once the infection settles, let me know and I’ll check it.
Thanks, doctor.

social.t: Keen swimmers and people who clean their ears with cotton buds get recurrent otitis externa. Changing the habit is the main prevention.
Temporary muffled hearing can affect work. Most people can work while treating it; a fit note is rarely needed.

legal.t: GMC Decision making and consent (2020): explain the benefits and risks of microsuction or wick insertion, including brief dizziness or discomfort, before going ahead.

professional.t: Follow the UKHSA prescribing summary: topical treatment first, oral antibiotics only for spreading cellulitis or systemic signs.

Avoid aminoglycoside drops with a perforation unless ENT specifically advises them; the ENT UK consensus (2007) conditions — obvious infection, no more than 2 weeks, risk explained — are a specialist exception. Record the drum status and your reasoning.

community.t: Many areas have community ear care or microsuction services that GPs can refer to for aural toilet when the canal is blocked.

redFlags: Severe or persistent pain, especially at night, out of proportion to the signs
Facial weakness or other cranial nerve palsy
Diabetes, immunosuppression or older age with non-resolving disease
ice: Concern: whether his hearing will come back

playbook.diagnosis: “This is otitis externa, an inflammation and infection of the skin of the ear canal, set off by swimming and kept going by the cotton buds.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “The skin in your ear canal is like the skin on a finger that’s been in water too long: soft and easy to damage. Once it’s scratched, germs get in and it swells, which is why it hurts to pull on the ear and why it sounds muffled.”

management.reflectIce: “You were expecting tablets. For this kind of ear infection, drops work better because they put the treatment right where it’s needed. And your hearing should come back as the swelling settles.”
management.psychosocial: Negotiate stopping cotton buds; time off swimming until settled; practical tips for showering; realistic time frame for relief.
sharedPlan: Aural toilet in the surgery, or microsuction referral if blocked; wick if the canal is too swollen
Topical acetic acid or antibiotic with or without steroid for 7 days (UKHSA summary; choice per BNF); non-aminoglycoside if the drum is not seen
Keep dry, no swimming until settled, stop cotton buds, treat any canal eczema
safetyNet: Return if not better after a week of drops
Same day if pain much worse or at night, redness spreading, fever, or facial weakness
Hearing check if it has not recovered after the infection settles
ENT referral if recurrent or not resolving

pitfalls.intro: The trap is prescribing tablets because he asks for them. The marks sit in topical treatment done well, prevention he will actually follow, and screening the rare dangerous variant.

items.fail: Prescribing oral antibiotics for uncomplicated otitis externa.
items.why: UKHSA summary: topical treatment; oral flucloxacillin only for spreading cellulitis or systemic signs.
items.fix: Drops or spray for 7 days, with analgesia.

items.fail: Giving drops into a canal full of debris.
items.why: The drops cannot reach the infected skin.
items.fix: Clean the canal first, or refer for microsuction or a wick.

items.fail: Using aminoglycoside drops when the drum cannot be seen, without thinking about it.
items.why: ENT UK consensus sets conditions for ototoxic drops with a perforation.
items.fix: Choose a non-aminoglycoside preparation; use an aminoglycoside only on ENT advice, and record why.

items.fail: Never asking about diabetes, immunosuppression, night pain or facial weakness.
items.why: These identify necrotising otitis externa, which needs same-day ENT.
items.fix: Ask the four questions and include them in the safety-net.

items.why: Habits change when the reason is understood and the plan feels realistic.
items.fix: Explain how buds keep it going and ask whether he can manage without them.

items.fail: “Come back if it doesn’t get better.”
items.why: Vague safety-netting is standard failing feedback.
items.fix: A week of drops; same-day return for night pain, spreading redness, fever or facial weakness.

Pain severity and night pain, discharge, fever, spreading redness, facial weakness, diabetes or immunosuppression, previous perforation, skin conditions.

wordPics.fail: Prescribes oral amoxicillin as for otitis media; never looks in the canal or asks about diabetes or night pain; no advice about cotton buds or keeping the ear dry.
wordPics.pass: Diagnoses otitis externa, prescribes topical treatment rather than tablets, advises keeping it dry and stopping cotton buds, and safety-nets.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: cleans the canal so drops work; chooses a safe preparation when the drum is not seen; teaches the technique; explains why drops beat tablets in his terms; answers his hearing worry; screens necrotising otitis externa features; teach-back.

avoid.dont: “I’ll give you a course of antibiotic tablets.”
avoid.instead: “Drops put the treatment right where the infection is, and work better for this.”
avoid.why: Oral antibiotics are not indicated for uncomplicated otitis externa (UKHSA summary).

avoid.dont: “Keep cleaning it with cotton buds so the drops get in.”
avoid.instead: “No cotton buds at all. I’ll clean it for you.”
avoid.why: Cotton buds damage the canal skin and perpetuate the infection.

avoid.instead: “Severe pain at night or facial weakness would need checking the same day.”
avoid.why: Necrotising otitis externa is a skull-base osteomyelitis and is easily missed.

Oral antibiotics are for spreading cellulitis or systemic illness, and severe persistent pain in a diabetic or immunocompromised person raises necrotising otitis externa.

points.t: Otalgia, itch, discharge, a blocked or muffled feeling, and pain on moving the tragus or pinna, with a red, swollen canal containing debris. Triggers: swimming and water exposure, trauma from cotton buds or fingers, hearing aids or earplugs, and skin conditions such as eczema, seborrhoeic dermatitis or psoriasis.

Otitis media gives deeper pain, often with a bulging or red drum and no tragal tenderness; discharge only follows a perforation. Also consider a furuncle (focal boil), a foreign body, and otomycosis (itch, fluffy white or black debris), which needs antifungal drops rather than antibiotics.

UKHSA summary [1]: analgesia and local heat; then topical acetic acid (over 12s) or a topical antibiotic with or without a steroid, which have similar cure rates at 7 days. Cochrane [4]: acetic acid is comparable at 1 week but less effective when treatment is longer. Choice and dosing per BNF. Do not give oral antibiotics for uncomplicated otitis externa [1][5].

Remove debris by dry mopping or refer for microsuction if the canal is blocked; a very swollen canal may need an ear wick placed by ENT or a trained clinician. Lie with the affected ear up for a few minutes after the drops go in.

If the drum is perforated or cannot be seen, avoid aminoglycoside drops unless ENT specifically advises them; the ENT UK consensus conditions (obvious infection, no more than 2 weeks, risks explained, ideally baseline audiometry) are a specialist exception [2]. Use a non-aminoglycoside preparation instead (per BNF and local formulary).
UKHSA summary [1]: if cellulitis spreads beyond the canal or there are systemic signs, give oral flucloxacillin (dose per BNF) and refer to exclude necrotising otitis externa.

UK consensus [3]: suspect it in people with diabetes, immunosuppression or older age who have severe or persistent pain (often worse at night) out of proportion to the signs, granulation tissue in the canal, or cranial nerve palsy, especially facial. It is a skull-base osteomyelitis needing same-day ENT assessment.

Stop cotton buds; keep the ear dry (no swimming until settled, protect the ear when showering); treat any canal eczema; after recovery, consider earplugs or a swimming cap and drying the ear gently. Recurrent or non-resolving disease needs review and ENT referral.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; let him describe pain, itch, discharge and muffled hearing; heard the swimming and cotton-bud history.
Swimming habit; how the blocked hearing affects him; willingness to stop cotton buds.
Picked up “hurts if I pull on it” as tragal tenderness and the cotton buds as a perpetuating cause.
Idea (infection), concern (hearing may not return), expectation (antibiotic tablets).
Pinna and tragal tenderness, otoscopy of canal and drum, skin around the ear, temperature; microsuction or wick if blocked.
Otitis externa versus otitis media, furuncle, foreign body, otomycosis, necrotising otitis externa.
Screened night pain, systemic features, spreading cellulitis, facial weakness, diabetes and immunosuppression.
Acute otitis externa of the right ear.
Aural toilet; 7 days of topical treatment per UKHSA summary; non-ototoxic choice when the drum is not seen; analgesia; no oral antibiotics.
Drop technique; keep dry; stop cotton buds; skin conditions; hearing concern answered.
Return if not better after a week, spreading redness, fever, night pain or facial weakness; hearing check if not recovered.

social.t: Keen swimmers and people who clean their ears with cotton buds get recurrent otitis externa. Changing the habit is the main prevention.
Temporary muffled hearing can affect work. Most people can work while treating it; a fit note is rarely needed.

legal.t: GMC Decision making and consent (2020): explain the benefits and risks of microsuction or wick insertion, including brief dizziness or discomfort, before going ahead.

professional.t: Follow the UKHSA prescribing summary: topical treatment first, oral antibiotics only for spreading cellulitis or systemic signs.

Avoid aminoglycoside drops with a perforation unless ENT specifically advises them; the ENT UK consensus (2007) conditions — obvious infection, no more than 2 weeks, risk explained — are a specialist exception. Record the drum status and your reasoning.

community.t: Many areas have community ear care or microsuction services that GPs can refer to for aural toilet when the canal is blocked.

redFlags: Severe or persistent pain, especially at night, out of proportion to the signs
Facial weakness or other cranial nerve palsy
Diabetes, immunosuppression or older age with non-resolving disease
ice: Concern: whether his hearing will come back

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This is otitis externa, an inflammation and infection of the skin of the ear canal, set off by swimming and kept going by the cotton buds.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “The skin in your ear canal is like the skin on a finger that’s been in water too long: soft and easy to damage. Once it’s scratched, germs get in and it swells, which is why it hurts to pull on the ear and why it sounds muffled.”

management.reflectIce: “You were expecting tablets. For this kind of ear infection, drops work better because they put the treatment right where it’s needed. And your hearing should come back as the swelling settles.”
management.psychosocial: Negotiate stopping cotton buds; time off swimming until settled; practical tips for showering; realistic time frame for relief.
sharedPlan: Aural toilet in the surgery, or microsuction referral if blocked; wick if the canal is too swollen
Topical acetic acid or antibiotic with or without steroid for 7 days (UKHSA summary; choice per BNF); non-aminoglycoside if the drum is not seen
Keep dry, no swimming until settled, stop cotton buds, treat any canal eczema
safetyNet: Return if not better after a week of drops
Same day if pain much worse or at night, redness spreading, fever, or facial weakness
Hearing check if it has not recovered after the infection settles
ENT referral if recurrent or not resolving

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The trap is prescribing tablets because he asks for them. The marks sit in topical treatment done well, prevention he will actually follow, and screening the rare dangerous variant.

items.fail: Prescribing oral antibiotics for uncomplicated otitis externa.
items.why: UKHSA summary: topical treatment; oral flucloxacillin only for spreading cellulitis or systemic signs.
items.fix: Drops or spray for 7 days, with analgesia.

items.fail: Giving drops into a canal full of debris.
items.why: The drops cannot reach the infected skin.
items.fix: Clean the canal first, or refer for microsuction or a wick.

items.fail: Using aminoglycoside drops when the drum cannot be seen, without thinking about it.
items.why: ENT UK consensus sets conditions for ototoxic drops with a perforation.
items.fix: Choose a non-aminoglycoside preparation; use an aminoglycoside only on ENT advice, and record why.

items.fail: Never asking about diabetes, immunosuppression, night pain or facial weakness.
items.why: These identify necrotising otitis externa, which needs same-day ENT.
items.fix: Ask the four questions and include them in the safety-net.

items.why: Habits change when the reason is understood and the plan feels realistic.
items.fix: Explain how buds keep it going and ask whether he can manage without them.

items.fail: “Come back if it doesn’t get better.”
items.why: Vague safety-netting is standard failing feedback.
items.fix: A week of drops; same-day return for night pain, spreading redness, fever or facial weakness.
